name: North Sikkim
tagline: Yak pastures, Lepcha villages and lakes above 5,000 m
meta_description: North Sikkim (Mangan district) trip guide: Lachung, Yumthang, Lachen, Gurudongmar, Dzongu. Permits, road status, altitude and honest 2026 prices.
summary: North Sikkim, officially Mangan district, is Sikkim's largest and emptiest district: Lepcha villages in Dzongu, the self-governing Bhutia villages of Lachung and Lachen, Yumthang's rhododendron valley and Gurudongmar Lake near the Tibet border. Go October–November or April–May, with permits, a registered agent and at least two nights.
intro: North Sikkim begins about 15 km out of Gangtok, just before Kabi, and runs north to the Tibetan plateau. In between, the North Sikkim Highway follows the Teesta past Phodong, Mangan and Chungthang, where the Lachen and Lachung rivers meet. Since December 2021 the district has been called Mangan district, after its headquarters town, but travellers and drivers still say North Sikkim. It is the largest district in the state and the least crowded: the 2011 census counted about 43,700 people, roughly ten per square kilometre.

Most visitors come for two valleys. The Lachung valley leads to Yumthang, a river meadow at about 3,564 m that flowers with rhododendron and primula from April, and on to Zero Point at about 4,660 m. The Lachen valley climbs past Thangu to Gurudongmar Lake, a sacred lake near the border at roughly 5,150–5,430 m. Both villages are governed by their own traditional councils, the Dzumsa, which is unique in India.

South of Mangan, across the Teesta, lies Dzongu, a reserve set aside for the Lepcha people, Sikkim's earliest known inhabitants. Here you stay with Lepcha families in homestays, walk among cardamom fields and, every three years, can join pilgrims walking to Tholung Monastery for the airing of its relics. Closer to Gangtok, Kabi Lungchok marks a 13th-century blood-brotherhood pact between the Lepcha and Bhutia, and Phodong and Labrang monasteries hold some of Sikkim's oldest murals.

North Sikkim is also fragile. In October 2023 a glacial lake outburst from South Lhonak Lake destroyed the Teesta III dam at Chungthang, and slides closed Lachen for long stretches in 2024–26. Roads are rebuilt, but every trip still depends on weather, permits and a registered vehicle. We plan around that honestly, and we tell you when not to go.

story.title: Two villages that govern themselves: the Dzumsa
story.text: Lachung and Lachen are the only villages in Sikkim that do not elect an ordinary gram panchayat. Instead, they are run by the Dzumsa (pronounced zom-sa), a traditional council of the Bhutia families of each village. Every household has a voice. The council chooses a headman, the Pipon, usually for a one-year term, who in turn appoints assistants known as Gyapon or Gyenbo. Together they settle disputes, organise work on shared land and pastures, fix fines, and decide matters that touch the whole community, including, in recent decades, how tourism works in the village. Wikipedia's article on the Dzumsa dates the present form of the system to the first half of the 19th century, when these high trading villages on the routes to Tibet needed a way to organise grazing, trade and seasonal moves. Rather than replace it, the state of Sikkim folded it into law. The Sikkim Panchayat (Amendment) Act of 1995 treated the Dzumsas of Lachen and Lachung as gram panchayats, and the 2001 amendment confirmed that they continue under their own traditional and customary law, with panchayat powers added on top. When you see a notice about plastic bottles at a Lachung hotel or a fixed rate for a service, it may well be a Dzumsa decision. Respect it: in these two villages, the council is the local government.
story.source: Wikipedia, Dzumsa; Sikkim Panchayat (Amendment) Acts 1995 and 2001; Mangan district administration (mangan.nic.in)

little_known.fact: Lepcha, not Nepali, is the most common first language in Mangan district: 31.7 percent of residents named it in the 2011 census, ahead of Nepali at 23.2 percent and Sikkimese (Bhutia) at 14.4 percent.
little_known.source: Census of India 2011, via Wikipedia, Mangan district

little_known.fact: Tumlong, just below Phodong on the North Sikkim Highway, was the capital of the Kingdom of Sikkim from 1793 after raids on Rabdentse, until the Chogyal's capital moved to Gangtok in the late 19th century.
The Shingba Rhododendron Sanctuary on the road to Yumthang was established in 1984 and covers about 43 square kilometres, protecting dozens of rhododendron species between roughly 3,000 and 4,000 m.
little_known.source: Wikipedia, Mangan district and Shingba Rhododendron Sanctuary

little_known.fact: Dzongu has been a reserved area for the Lepcha people since a royal proclamation of the Chogyal era, generally dated to 1956, under which people from other communities may not settle or buy land there.

The October 2023 flood that destroyed the 1,200 MW Teesta III dam at Chungthang started at South Lhonak Lake, a glacial lake that grew from about 17 hectares in 1977 to more than 160 hectares by 2023.

facts: Mangan (≈ 956 m), ≈ 67 km · 2.5–3 h from Gangtok
Protected area permit via a registered agent for Lachung and Lachen; Dzongu permit for the Lepcha reserve

highlights.title: Yumthang Valley and Zero Point
highlights.text: A river meadow at about 3,564 m, reached through the Shingba rhododendron forests 24 km above Lachung. From late April it flowers pink, red and white; in winter it lies under snow. Zero Point (Yumesamdong), 23 km further at about 4,660 m, is where the civilian road ends.

highlights.title: Gurudongmar Lake
highlights.text: A glacier-fed lake near the Tibet border, sacred to Buddhists, who link it with Guru Padmasambhava. The Sikkim government gives its altitude as 5,430 m. It freezes from about November to May, and is reached only on a pre-dawn drive from Lachen, Indians only.

highlights.title: Dzongu Lepcha homestays
highlights.text: Stay with Lepcha families inside the reserve across the Teesta from Mangan. Walk among large cardamom fields, eat nettle soup and millet, and hear how Dzongu's young people opposed big dams in 2007–08 and then built a homestay economy.

highlights.title: Lachung, a Dzumsa village
highlights.text: Joseph Hooker called Lachung the most picturesque village of Sikkim in his Himalayan Journals. Its wooden houses, apple orchards and 1880 Nyingma monastery sit at about 2,700 m, and the village is still governed by its traditional Dzumsa council.

highlights.title: Phodong and Labrang monasteries
highlights.text: Two monasteries 2 km apart on a ridge 38 km from Gangtok: Phodong, a Karma Kagyu seat with old murals and a December masked dance, and Labrang, a Nyingma monastery completed in the 1840s that keeps much of its original structure.

highlights.title: Kabi Lungchok
highlights.text: A grove of standing stones 17 km from Gangtok where, in Sikkimese tradition, the Lepcha chief Thekong Tek and the Bhutia prince Khye Bumsa swore blood brotherhood in the 13th century before Kangchenjunga as witness. Life-size statues of both now stand at the site.

getting_there: There is no airport or railway in Mangan district. Fly to Bagdogra (IXB) or take a train to New Jalpaiguri (NJP), then drive 4.5–5 hours to Gangtok on NH10, which closes after monsoon landslides; the alternative is via Kalimpong or Algarah. Spend a night in Gangtok: it helps with altitude and lets your agent file permits. From Gangtok, the North Sikkim Highway runs north via Kabi (17 km), Phodong (38 km) and Mangan (67 km) to Chungthang (about 95 km), where it splits for Lachung and Lachen, each about 120 km and 5–6 hours from Gangtok. Tourist vehicles must cross the Toong check post by 4:00 pm. Pakyong Airport has had no scheduled flights since June 2024. Check current status before you travel.
permits: Indian travellers need a protected area permit for Lachung, Yumthang, Zero Point, Lachen, Thangu and Gurudongmar, issued only through Sikkim Tourism-registered agents and tied to a registered tourist vehicle; operators require a minimum two-night stay. Dzongu needs its own permit, usually obtained in Mangan. Children under five are not permitted in North Sikkim protected areas. Foreign nationals need the online Sikkim restricted area permit and may visit Lachung, Yumthang and Zero Point on a group permit, but not Gurudongmar; for Lachen and Thangu, ask us. Check current status before you travel.
money: On a budget, a 2-night/3-day shared North Sikkim package from Gangtok costs about ₹6,500–9,000 per person with a jeep seat, permit, simple hotel or homestay and meals; add ₹3,000–4,000 per vehicle for Zero Point. Dzongu homestays cost about ₹1,500–2,500 per person a night with meals. At mid level, a private SUV for 2N/3D runs about ₹16,000–24,000 per vehicle, plus value or comfort hotels at ₹3,000–8,000 a room. At the top, Yarlam Resort in Lachung costs roughly ₹9,000–15,000 a room. Carry cash: ATMs exist in Mangan, Lachung and Lachen but often fail. All figures are indicative 2026 rates.

months.weather: Lachung −5 to 8 °C, snow likely; Mangan 5 to 16 °C
months.summary: Deep winter. Lachung often has snow on the ground, which is why some families choose January, but the road to Yumthang closes for days at a time and Zero Point is usually out of reach. Lachen and Gurudongmar are frequently shut; the lake is frozen. Lower down, Mangan, Dzongu and Phodong are cool and clear, with good Kangchenjunga views from Singhik. Namsoong celebrations at Namprikdang can run into early January.
months.tip: Keep one spare day in the plan; a single snowfall can close the Lachung road overnight.

months.weather: Lachung −4 to 9 °C, snow likely; Mangan 6 to 18 °C
months.summary: Still winter in the high valleys, with snow at Lachung and closures above Yumthang common. Lachung and Lachen families celebrate Losar, the Tibetan new year, in February or March, a family occasion rather than a show. The lower district is dry and bright: a good month for Phodong, Labrang and Kabi Lungchok as easy day trips from Gangtok.
months.tip: Thermals, gloves and a woollen cap are essential for any night above Mangan.

months.weather: Lachung 0 to 12 °C; Yumthang often snowbound early in the month
months.summary: The thaw begins. Early-season visitors may see snow at Yumthang with the first rhododendrons flowering lower down, though road closures after late snowfall are still possible. Lachen and Gurudongmar access depends on that year's road status and snow. Crowds are thin and prices are lower than in April and May.
months.tip: Book flexible hotels in March; late snow can still cancel a Yumthang morning.

months.summary: Rhododendron season begins in earnest in the Shingba sanctuary and Yumthang, usually peaking from late April into May. Days are mild, though afternoons cloud over. This is the traditional season for the Tholung Kamsel when it falls due, and Dzongu is green and comfortable. Book Lachung hotels early.
months.tip: Start Yumthang by 6 am to see the flowers before the cloud comes in.

months.summary: Peak spring and peak demand. Yumthang is in full flower, Zero Point usually opens, and Gurudongmar starts to thaw at the edges when Lachen is open. Indian school holidays fill hotels and shared jeeps, so book weeks ahead. Pre-monsoon showers arrive late in the month.
months.tip: Reserve Lachung and Lachen rooms at least three weeks ahead for May.

months.weather: Lachung 10 to 19 °C, heavy rain; slides common
months.summary: The monsoon arrives. Yumthang turns green with primulas and wildflowers, but landslides close the North Sikkim Highway often, sometimes for days, and many operators stop selling Lachen. We do not recommend North Sikkim trips from mid-June. Phodong and Kabi remain possible as short trips from Gangtok.
months.tip: If you must travel, buy refundable tickets and keep two buffer days.

months.weather: Lachung 11 to 19 °C, very wet; frequent slides
months.summary: The wettest stretch. Road closures above Mangan are common, leeches are out in Dzongu, and the waterfalls along the highway, including Seven Sisters and Naga, are at full roar. Short visits close to Gangtok are fine. Plan the high valleys for October instead.
months.tip: Waterfalls are best viewed from the road; do not climb wet rocks.

months.summary: Monsoon continues, with breaks of clear weather. Closures and permit suspensions are frequent: in 2026 the Lachen road was repaired only on 29 August. Day trips to Kabi Lungchok and Phodong remain the safest options. Pang Lhabsol falls in late August or September in Gangtok.
months.tip: Watch for permit announcements late in the month before booking anything north of Mangan.

months.summary: The rains ease and the valleys reopen. Lachung and Yumthang are green and quiet, and in 2026 Lachen permits resumed around 11–12 September. Showers and slides are still possible in the first half. Late September brings clearer skies and the first autumn colour above Lachung.
months.tip: Choose the second half of September for drier roads.

months.summary: Our favourite month. Skies are clearest, Kangchenjunga stands out from Singhik, and the drive to Gurudongmar is cold but bright. Larch and maple turn gold above Lachung late in the month. It is also a busy Indian holiday season around Durga Puja and Diwali, so book early.
months.tip: Book around Puja and Diwali dates at least a month in advance.

months.weather: Lachung −1 to 12 °C; Gurudongmar starting to freeze
months.summary: Cold, dry and clear, with fewer crowds after Diwali. Gurudongmar begins to freeze from the edges, and Zero Point often has fresh snow. Dzongu is pleasant for walking, and the 2021 Tholung Kamsel was held in late November. Nights in Lachen and Lachung drop to around freezing.
months.tip: Pack down jackets for Gurudongmar mornings, which can be −10 °C with wind.

months.weather: Lachung −4 to 9 °C, snow possible; Mangan 6 to 17 °C
months.summary: Winter arrives in the high valleys, with the first proper snow at Lachung, and Gurudongmar trips often stop. Lower down, it is festival season: the Phodong chaam on the 28th and 29th days of the 10th Tibetan month, and the Lepcha Namsoong at Namprikdang near Mangan at the turn of the year.
months.tip: Combine the Phodong chaam with a Dzongu homestay for Namsoong week.

faqs.q: Is North Sikkim open for tourists in 2026?
faqs.a: As we understand it, Lachung, Yumthang and Zero Point reopened on 8 September 2025. Lachen and Gurudongmar reopened on 9 March 2026, closed in April after a landslide, and permits resumed around 11–12 September 2026 after road repairs on 29 August. Weather can close roads at short notice, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for North Sikkim?
faqs.a: At least two nights, which is also the operators' minimum: one night in Lachen for Gurudongmar and one in Lachung for Yumthang. Three nights is better, allowing a slower pace or a Dzongu homestay. Add at least one night in Gangtok before, for acclimatisation and permit paperwork, and one after as a buffer.

faqs.q: How do I get a North Sikkim permit?
faqs.a: Indian travellers need a protected area permit, issued only through a Sikkim Tourism-registered agent and linked to a registered tourist vehicle. Give your agent ID and two passport photos a day or two ahead. Dzongu has a separate permit, usually issued in Mangan. Foreign nationals face more limits. Check current status before you travel.

Partly. With the online Sikkim restricted area permit and a protected area permit through a registered agent, in a group of two or more, foreigners can usually visit Lachung, Yumthang and Zero Point. Gurudongmar Lake is closed to foreigners. Rules for Lachen and Thangu are unclear at present, so ask us. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I take a child under five to North Sikkim?
faqs.a: No. Children under five are not permitted in North Sikkim protected areas, which include Lachung, Yumthang, Zero Point, Lachen and Gurudongmar. With small children, consider Gangtok, Phodong, Kabi Lungchok and Mangan, which lie outside the protected areas, or the hills of West and South Sikkim instead.

faqs.q: What does a North Sikkim trip cost in 2026?
faqs.a: Indicatively, a 2-night/3-day shared package from Gangtok costs about ₹6,500–9,000 per person with jeep seat, permit, simple stays and meals. A private SUV for the same trip is about ₹16,000–24,000 per vehicle, plus hotels. Zero Point adds about ₹3,000–4,000 per vehicle. Comfort and premium hotels raise costs considerably.

faqs.q: Is altitude sickness a risk in North Sikkim?
faqs.a: Yes. Lachung and Lachen are about 2,700–2,750 m, Yumthang about 3,564 m, Zero Point about 4,660 m and Gurudongmar around 5,150–5,430 m. Climb gradually, sleep low, drink plenty of water and avoid alcohol. Headache, nausea and breathlessness are warning signs: descend if they worsen. Consult a doctor first if you have heart or lung conditions.

faqs.q: What is the best month to visit North Sikkim?
faqs.a: October and November give the clearest skies, the best mountain views and dry roads, though they are cold at Gurudongmar. April and May bring the rhododendron bloom at Yumthang and milder days. Avoid June to August, when landslides close roads often. December to March is for snow lovers, with frequent closures.

faqs.q: Can I stay in Dzongu instead of Lachung?
faqs.a: Yes, and many travellers combine both. Dzongu is a Lepcha reserve with family homestays, much lower and warmer than Lachung, and needs its own permit. It does not replace the high valleys of Yumthang and Gurudongmar, but it offers a slower, more personal side of North Sikkim. Two nights is ideal.
